speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, the Unemployment Insurance Act requires the government to
review annually the rate of premiums to be paid by employers and employees during the year ahead.
With the completion of tabulation of the T4 returns for 1972, processed by the Department of National Revenue in September, 1973, and analysed by the commission, we now have accurate and complete financial data for last year. For 1972 the insurable earnings base was $42 billion, 36 per cent of this being the wages or salaries of persons covered by unemployment insurance for the first time and paying a preferential rate; the employer-employee contribution, just recently determined, was $691 million. The cost chargeable to the employer-employee account is now known to be $1,104 million. Earned interest is $2.8 million.
Thus there was an operating deficit of $410 million on this account for the calendar year of 1972. The opening cash balance as of January 1, 1972, carried over from the old unemployment insurance fund, was $235.5 million. This was applied against that deficit.
For 1973, we now forecast the total benefit payments at $2,050 million. This, together with administrative costs, interest payments, less overpayments recovered, will bring the total cash flow requirements to $2,201 million. Of this, $932 million will be the government's share, and $1,269 million is chargeable to the employee-employer premium account.
This year the shortfall of charges to the employee-employer premium account over premium revenue is expected to be about $335 million. Adding this figure to the net cash deficit of $174.5 million as of last December 31 will result in a cumulative deficit of about $509.6 million in the employee-employer account by the end of 1973.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: What's half a million?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Based upon this analysis, we have recommended and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has approved, these contribution rates for the calendar year 1974: For employees, $1.40 per $100 of insurable earnings; for employers, $1.96 per $100 of insurable earnings.
At the new rates, the employee-employer account can be expected to break even for operations in the calendar year 1974, and could produce some surplus to reduce the cumulative deficit. In 1975 there will be between $100 million and $120 million in new and additional revenue as a result of the disappearance of the preferential rate, which will mean a very substantial reduction in the deficit that year. These new rates are adequate to retire the current deficit at least by the end of 1978, barring unforeseen adverse economic developments.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the new act was passed in 1971 it was obvious that the old structure of the Unemployment Insurance Commission would not be adequate to cope with the new universal coverage, the different definitions of eligibility, the range of special benefits, and other changes that made the new program radically different from the outmoded one it replaced.
In an ideal world-

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
-the desirable, cautious approach would have been to design and set up the new organization and give it a year's dry run before implementing the new act in order to work out the snags and loopholes, and to compile the data necessary for precise calculation of its costs, and the fine tuning of the premiums necessary to pay the portion of these costs shared by employers and employees.
But I need hardly remind hon. members, who I thought would be interested in a full disclosure, that in 1971 in Canada unemployment was at its recent peak. Over the year it averaged 6.4 per cent. To hold back the launching of the new program until all systems had been triplechecked and tested would have been to put administrative tidiness ahead of real human need. The government's choice was to introduce the program on an urgent basis- the new benefit rules went into effect June 27, only five days after passage of the bill-rebuilding the administrative structure and redesigning its operations as it went along. Of course, the high unemployment that made the changeover so urgent added substantially to the problems it entailed.
The problems that did develop fell into two main categories: inadequate service to claimants and inadequate control to protect the program from payment of benefits to persons not entitled to receive them.
While the commission began attacking both problem areas, it was clear that priority had to be given to service. In fairness, control measures could only be fully reinforced after it had been assured that every person entitled to receive benefits was in fact getting them, and getting them on time.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Clearly the old, mail-order operation of the commission was no longer appropriate. It was in fact a major weakness of the system.
With this in mind, and following many of the recommendations of my predecessor, I laid special stress on more efficient, sensitive and personalized service when I announced in April a major reorganization and decentralization of commission operations and head office. The reorganization, which included the opening of 20 new offices and upgrading some 100 existing offices and satellites,

essentially transformed our operations from an assembly line into a network of compact working units in which clients and staff deal mainly face to face. By the end of the year, practically all our 359 working units will be in place in our various locations.
Along with the structural and procedural changes, a comprehensive and successful training program has been completed, involving 100,000 hours for commission personnel, an investment that is paying off in service and in the attitude of our people to clients.
In addition to better service, this whole reorganization is intended equally to prevent the payment of benefits to persons not entitled. Concurrently, over the last year, we have been expanding our benefit control staff greatly. It was 147 a year ago. It is now 369 and will be 424 before the end of the year. Our benefit control investigations have resulted in disqualifications, disentitlements, or both, of 200,000 claimants so far this year and the total is expected to reach a quarter of a million by the end of the year. By contrast, the total for all of 1972 was 65,000.
Benefit control investigation, as such, is only one of several programs followed to ensure that benefits are paid only to those entitled to receive them. I am referring to such measures as the active job search, information concerning job refusals, and our post-audits. Through these, and over all, our disentitlements and disqualifications have increased by close to 50 per cent from 1972 to 1973.
To further ensure that the need for strict control is observed as fully as the need for efficient service, we are now taking several additional steps: First, a stepped-up information program to ensure that claimants are fully informed not only of their rights but also of their obligations, including the obligation to carry on an active job search and to be available for work, as an essential condition of entitlement to regular benefits. Second, to assure balance between service and control, additional insurance officers were appointed to interview personally, at the initial stage of a claim, selected categories of claimants. Among the categories to be interviewed are persons who have left their jobs voluntarily, claimants who have transferred from special maternity or sickness benefits to regular benefits, persons who have their unemployment insurance claims transferred from one part of the country to another, and claimants whose occupational skills are in high demand in their locality. These interviews will begin with an initial monthly target of 60,000 people in December, increasing to 95,000 by March.
Thus, as many as 50 or 60 per cent of our claimants will be directly reminded of their obligations, as well as of their rights, through these interviews. This was not done before. Nor was it practical or possible to do so until the reorganization took place this year.
We shall be maintaining close liaison with Canada Manpower Centres to ensure that the unemployed person receives the promptest possible referral to a job opening and that these referrals are followed up until the claimant has the best possible form of income maintenance-a new job and a regular pay cheque.

November 7, 1973

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: All these control requirements will be in place before the end of the year. I am confident they will eliminate most of the remaining misuse of any significance. Because of this administrative vigilance and the effective protection it offers against the kind of abuse Bill C-125 was originally intended to correct, I have decided against proceeding further with that particular bill at this time.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
The important review of social security in Canada now going on under the leadership of my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, also makes this the wrong time for a legislative change in a social program as significant as the unemployment insurance program. Nevertheless, we are pressing ahead with the analysis of the many briefs and representations we have received in connection with the legislation, all in the light of the much better data now available and the experience of the first full year's operation of the new act.
I have said, and I repeat, that the program is good. But as a result of a year's experience and a better information base we shall be in a much better position now to determine and bring forward the kind of legislative changes that may be beneficial.
In the light of our experience this year, I believe the main specific purpose for which Bill C-125 was introduced, namely, to deal with the situation in which persons voluntarily quit their jobs without cause, can be better achieved by vigilant and selective administrative action rather than by rigid and perhaps punitive changes in the law. However, I must warn that the administrative approach will indeed be vigilant. Anyone who thinks the decision with regard to Bill C-125 is any hint of laxity in control on the part of the Unemployment Insurance Commission is in for a rude awakening.
I am determined-and I hope all hon. members will join me in this determination-that the unemployed who are genuinely doing their best to get work will receive their rightful benefits and our fullest assistance in their efforts to find new jobs.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: But, Mr. Speaker-and I hope all hon. members will join me in this, too-I am equally determined to protect the integrity of this plan and ensure that those who are not entitled to benefits will not receive them. I am confident we now have the administrative system and the competence to make this determination stick.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I see that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) wants to get into the act. I want to let him know that the unemployment insurance bill, C-125, that was brought into the House of Commons was one of the greatest fiascoes with which this House has ever had to contend.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Before I go further I do want to be fair to the minister in one regard. I want to thank him for making his statement available. I believe it was submitted
Unemployment Insurance
around 1.15 p.m., which certainly is an all-time record for this government. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) says he has known longer times, but I thank the minister for that anyway.
The fact that the minister has now admitted that disen-titlements and disqualifications could reach a quarter of a million by the end of the year certainly shows that in the first instance the act should never have been passed without it having been given a dry run and unless we were quite sure of its administrative tidiness. The minister indicates that he preferred to see those who were in need get assistance. But what he forgot to say was that those who were in need never did get it.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
It took the prompting of the opposition through questions, speeches and motions to bring the government to its senses and make it attempt to tidy up the legislation. At that time improvements were made. But what shocks me again is that the minister implied that, because the Minister of National Health and Welfare is now considering certain legislation with respect to social welfare, he cannot bring in any amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I think this is irresponsible. If the minister believes there should be amendments made to the Unemployment Insurance Act, then what the Minister of National Health and Welfare has to say has nothing to do with the minister trying to improve the commission which at this time is in a mess.
One of the most disastrous things we have done in this House was to remove the $800 million statutory ceiling. This means that members of the opposition and the people of Canada can never tell in what state the unemployment insurance fund is at any particular time unless the minister stands up and makes a statement. Thank goodness that he will be bringing in his estimates soon, at which time we will be able to probe quite deeply and raise very important questions.
I am surprised to note that the minister did not take it upon himself to answer in his statement the several very important questions that were raised by the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Ellis), who in a very critical analysis made some points that should have been answered by the minister. I refer to the $1 billion in connection with overpayments and frauds, the increase in staff from 5,200 to 13,000, the failure of the commission to account publicly for $857 million in emergency funds, the attempt by the UIC to disguise overspending by deleting from its monthly reports statistical information that it used to list giving amounts spent in previous months and years.
I do not know why the minister did not have the courage to answer those questions. They are extremely important and he will have to answer them as soon as his estimates go before the committee.
I am also very surprised that the minister did not bear down on a particular sequence of events which are making a number of people in Canada, particularly members of the opposition, very concerned, especially in regard to the minister's estimates. He has indicated that the plan will cost $2,050 million for the year 1973, but at no time did he

November 7, 1973
Unemployment Insurance
tell us what the unemployment rate would be in 1973.1 fail to understand how he can give us projections without telling us what the unemployment rate is or will be. This is an extremely important point.
We now find that job vacancies are rising. We find we are suffering from higher unemployment. There are higher benefit and administrative costs within the Unemployment Insurance Commission program. The minister has not attempted to correlate these or to advise the House whether a study is being made in order to show what is the relationship between the high job vacancy rate, rising unemployment and UIC costs. This is a question that has been asked by employers across the country who advise that the disincentive aspects of the act in fact are eroding the free enterprise system. I do not make light of that claim. It seems to me that in many instances, notwithstanding what the minister says, because of the inadequacy of this act people are prepared to take advantage of unemployment insurance when in fact they should be working, although sometimes we cannot blame them.
The minister indicated today that the program will cost more than $2 billion, much more than in 1972. What the minister did not say-I am continually reminded of the actuarial soundness of this plan by his predecessor who has pronounced that time and time again-was that the projected figure for administrative costs in 1971 was $71 million while the actual figure turned out to be $119 million. In 1972 these costs jumped to $122 million and in 1973 to $145 million.
I do not have much confidence as the minister has in the economy which to me is certainly being mismanaged. This act can work only if in fact we have a full employment policy, because without it we are approaching unemployment insurance as an ad hoc measure. We can only reduce the cost if the government will take it upon itself to introduce such a policy. We must have a full employment policy in order to decrease the run on the unemployment insurance fund.
I am also very surprised that the minister did not bring to our attention what is wrong with the illusive advisory committee. This committee was set up by the minister in order to probe allegations of harassment and to look into other related matters in respect of the UIC. I think, and I believe most people think, that this is an extremely important committee. I cannot understand why we have not had a report from the advisory committee to assist us. I say to the minister that he must start demanding rather than asking this committee to do its job. We need the information. We need the report.
I am very surprised also that the minister did not make any reference to holiday pay and severance pay. I understood that in conjunction with Bill C-125 he was going to bring in regulations in this regard. Severance pay was not to be included and only the first two weeks of holiday pay would be taken as income. Is that dead too? I wish the minister had answered that.
What we have now is an increase in the premium which is certainly an unwarranted tax. It is up to $1.40 for employees and I believe it was about $1.19 before. This is an unwarranted tax because of government mismanage-

ment What disturbs me is that this plan was supposed to be actuarially sound, meaning that all the contingencies had been looked into and it was possible for the government to bring out projections as to what it would cost and what the premiums would be. In every instance the government has been wrong. That is why I say the bill, which in the first instance some hon. members thought would be a good one, was a fraud of some significant impact upon the House of Commons and the people of Canada.
There are, of course, some matters on which the minister should be congratulated, particularly the stepped-up information program to ensure that claimants are fully informed. This is needed. I hope that with the further employment of benefit control officers these officers will be given instructions to deal with claimants in a humane and compassionate way. It seems to me that in too many instances benefit control officers are only being used to further the government's cause. I say that with some deliberation, and after some thought, Mr. Speaker. I trust the minister will advise these officers that those in need should not be unduly harassed and that they should get humane treatment. There are still too many people writing personally to me and to my office, saying that after working for 35 years and having paid the premiums they now find it extremely difficult to get their unemployment insurance benefits.
The minister's statement also indicates that an additional measure is close liaison with Canada Manpower Centres. This is a policy which should be adopted in full. Canada Manpower and the UIC should be blended into one, as this is the only way in which a claimant can acquire the necessary services and assistance that he needs.
In the long run the only way we can determine what is happening with respect to unemployment insurance is to have the ability to probe for information from the minister. In this regard I hope that the minister in future will give us a greater opportunity, because of the removal of the ceiling, to get involved with the UIC by asking him questions on the state of the fund.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that we accept the minister's statement. We are pleased that he was in a position to give us some answers with respect to the several problems that exist. But we cannot have confidence in the minister as to the cost of the plan because he has not advised us what the unemployment rate will be for the balance of the year, not to mention the inflation rate. Further, we are afraid that if a quarter of a million people have to be disqualified or disentitled there must be something wrong with the act. The program should be tightened up in order to make it more acceptable and in order to see to it that the Canadian people are not paying out money needlessly.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make clear at the outset that my colleagues and I are in favour of a decent unemployment insurance program and are therefore in favour of the general thrust of the unemployment insurance program that we have now.
November 7, 1973

I listened to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), Mr. Speaker, and in almost every sentence he went both ways at the same time.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION

It is all very well to say that the act was a catastrophe, a disaster, when it was passed and that it should never have been passed. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the government which was responsible for the high unemployment that we had in 1971 would have been doubly responsible, not only for mismanagement of the economy but for complete inhumanity, had it not brought that act into existence and implemented it even though the administration had not been entirely cleared up.
I have made clear on many occasions on behalf of our party that we do not condone, indeed we condemn as does every Canadian, any attempt by any person to misuse this program or any program that is on the statute books of this country, whether it is unemployment insurance, old age pensions or welfare. I would also like to point out that we in this party condemn the abuse by corporations of the various tax allowances to which they are entitled-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
-about which certain members of this House are always very silent. I do not know of any scheme provided by men, applicable to men and women, that is not abused by some section of the community. We congratulate the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the minister for having taken steps to tighten up the administration. I also congratulate him for not pursuing Bill C-125. I am in entire agreement with the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. Muir) who uttered the following words on October 29, addressed to the government House leader, as recorded at page 7304 of Hansard:
In view of the continuing difficulties being experienced by those, particularly in the Atlantic provinces, who have truly legitimate claims for unemployment insurance benefits in receiving such benefits, would the leader of the House give us his assurance that Bill C-125 will be cremated without ceremony and not brought back before the House?
My colleagues and I fully agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys. He made that statement because of his experience in his area and because of the human approach he has to the problem of unemployment, which some members of this House do not show.
I want to say to the minister, Mr. Speaker, that he is far too complacent about the way in which his benefit control officers are functioning. The suggestion in his statement that on the whole they are treating the legitimate claimants for unemployment insurance well, and that these legitimate claimants have no reason to complain, is far too complacent a statement. While it is true that the number of complaints we have received in our offices has been lower than it was some months ago, it is still a fact that many of the benefit control officers are acting in an insensitive and bureaucratic way, harassing genuine unemployment insurance claimants, and so far as my colleagues and I are concerned we will not be satisfied until that harassment of legitimate unemployment insur-
Unemployment Insurance
ance claimants completely disappears from the operations of the UIC.
I am very worried about the numbers that have been disqualified or disentitled this year, with an expectation that a quarter of a million will have been disqualified by the end of the year. To the extent that those people were abusing the program, my colleagues and I are totally in agreement with tightening up the administration. But to the extent that there have been disqualifications and dis-entitlements because people could not leave their homes in one community when they were told to go 50 or 60 miles away where there was a job available-and that situation has arisen-and to the extent that people left their homes and went to places where they found jobs were not available-to the extent that this quarter of a million involves some thousands of these cases, as I am sure it does, of people who have been unfairly treated, it is shameful for the commission, and indeed for the minister, to boast about it.
An unemployment insurance program is essential in any community for a redistribution of income, to make sure that people get some rights, even when they are unemployed, and to make sure that they have a means of living. My reading of the act tells me that the maximum benefit has been increased to $107 almost, will go up again to about $113, and that that increased benefit has to be paid for.
We agree with the principle that the proportion of the plan up to 4 per cent, which now has to be paid by employer-employee contributions, should be paid by those contributions. I am not convinced that the 40 cents increase is necessary, or that it might not have been 20 cents or 25 cents, but no doubt that is something a parliamentary committee will go into. But the principle that the increased benefit should be paid for, up to the 4 per cent level, is contained in the act and we accept it.
There are two things we regret. We regret that the government rejected our proposal that the cut-off line should be 3 per cent rather than 4 per cent, because 3 per cent is the line at which most economists consider we have more or less full employment. To have tacked on another percentage point, to be paid for by employers and employees, is something that we consider unfair and unnecessary.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I say to the minister and to the government that the only way to avoid the costs of unemployment insurance, to the extent that we now have them, is to have a full employment policy. The real condemnation of the government is that in the month of October we still had 6.2 per cent, seasonally adjusted, unemployed people in the work force of Canada. The only way to improve the situation is to go for a full employment policy, something which the government has not pursued. We reject, as strongly as I can find words to do it, the antiwelfare, the anti-unemployment insurance backlash for which the Tory party in this parliament is responsible.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON STATE OF FUND, NEW CONTRIBUTION RATES AND REORGANIZATION OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have preferred receiving this statement a

November 7, 1973
Unemployment Insurance
few minutes earlier as this would have allowed me to make relevant remarks under the circumstances.
The minister says in his statement that he sees a possibility of making up the deficit in 1978, if of course there are no mistakes such as those which occurred a few months after the passing of the legislation-because the mistakes which occurred at that time greatly distorted the estimates. For several days, we discussed the possibility of replenishing the unemployment insurance fund because the law did not make the necessary allowances.
This statement also mentions the adjustment of premiums for employers and employees. There is now much more effort to improve a system which caused so many delays harmful to the unemployed. Since its implementation, its mechanism completely defied common sense in certain instances. There is no need to go very far to find proof of this when hundreds of unemployed have to wait one, two, and even three months before receiving their unemployment insurance cheques. This happened in my constituency of Kamouraska and I believe that it also happened all through Quebec and probably Canada. Thousands of cases were brought to my attention last winter. Faulty administration of the law caused all types of payments to be made: excessive payments, double payments, reduced payments, and no payments. This makes four different types of payments. This is why I say-and I said it some time ago when I spoke in this House about the unemployment issue-that the law should be amended and made more flexible in its application.
In the present Unemployment Insurance Act-I should like to point this out immediately to the minister, because even though I read his statement quickly, I note that there is no such mention. It is provided that if the unemployed must wait too long, he can while waiting apply for assistance to the Quebec Department of Social Affairs. Is it possible to imagine a more stupid legislation! In such circumstances, they cannot even be paid! The legislation describes all kinds of periods: waiting period, supplementary period, extension period and we could even add without fear of being mistaken, a delay period. In his statement, the minister says that the system will be improved adn that steps will be taken to that effect. I do not blame the officials who administer it, because I had the opportunity to meet several in carrying out my work. Generally, the personnel work well, although some are putting off while others are idle. However in my opinion, the legislation is faulty, since it compels officials to adjust themselves and give stupid answers.
If I had had the time to study this statement a little better, I would have brought forward astounding proof that a bad legislation compels civil servants to pick their brains to give insignificant answers. Then, why not amend such a legislation and make it more flexible?
The minister also mentioned that the number of investigators had been increased in order to avoid frauds. But I would advise the minister to keep a sharp eye on the manner in which these investigators are prepared to discharge their duty.
The main purpose is so easily determined. God knows I met many investigators! Their main objective is to protect the fund and not the unemployed. If one of these investigators has other aims but to protect the fund, tell me his

name. It is primarily what the investigator does. With an army of investigators acting this way, it will not be possible to give satisfaction to Canadians.
Once the few improvements to the act have become law, I hope that my colleagues and I will be able to see the results. I do not think that we have good reasons to cheer the minister for his statement as some did earlier. Good intentions will do for the moment but let us wait for the results.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I wish to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Information from the Department of Finance and individual fishermen confirms representations I have made in the House, that chartered banks are ignoring government guaranteed loan programs and are actually deluding fishermen by charging rates of interest in excess of those provided under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. That the matter of government guaranteed loans be referred to the Standing Committees on Finance, Fisheries and Forestry and Consumer and Corporate Affairs and that an order be issued to call as witnesses the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the presidents of chartered banks to explain their unlawful practices which affect fishermen and consumers who are Canadian citizens.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-CFB SHEARWATER
speechtext: The primary role of CFB Shearwater is to contribute to Maritime Command's surveillance and control responsibilities by operating helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft from the base and by providing helicopter detachments for helicopter-destroyers. Additionally it provides airfield and ship berthing facilities for authorized military and civil aircraft and ships.

speechtext:
1.	Have proposals been received from, or on behalf of, Iraqui Airlines for the establishment of direct, regularly scheduled air service between Iraq and Canada and, if so (a) on what dates (b) what was the response to such suggestions?

4.	What has been the response thereto?

subsubtopic: NEGOTIATIONS RELATING TO CANADA-MIDDLE EAST AIR SERVICES
speechtext:
The Canadian Transport Commission and the Ministry of Transport (for question 2 only) advise as follows: 1. Yes; (a) May 29, 1973; (b) After interdepartmental consultation, a Canadian reply was made on July 16, 1973 advising the Iraqui Embassy that due to a current review of Canadian air policy and requests already received from other countries, a period of time would elapse before Canada would be in a position to negotiate. At the appropriate time we would get in touch with the Iraqui authorities.
2. It is the position of the government that there should be expanded commercial air contacts with various parts of
Order Paper Questions
the world, including the Middle East, where traffic warrants regular services by a Canadian airline and such services can be operated on an economic basis, and when satisfactory agreements can be negotiated. At the present time services are operated to Israel, and a first round of negotiations has been held with Lebanon.
3 and 4. Although airlines from time to time make approaches concerning scheduled services, only those requests received from governments are considered official. Taking this into consideration the following Middle East countries have requested negotiations: Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan: a note dated September 5, 1971 was received from the Jordanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs to the Canadian Embassy requesting negotiations. The Embassy reply of December 10, 1971 indicated that it appeared that traffic did not warrant a scheduled service but that Canada would continue to review the situation. United Arab Republic: The Minister of the Embassy of the United Arab Republic was informed by External Affairs on August 14, 1970 that Canada would be prepared to enter into negotiations if it were the wish of his government. To date there has been no official response. Lebanon: Following a meeting on August 13, 1970, as with the UAR, the Lebanese Ambassador requested negotiations. The first round of discussions took place on August 19 and 20, 1971 in Ottawa. The CTC is awaiting a mutually acceptable date for resumption of talks. Turkey: A bilateral air agreement with Turkey was signed May 21, 1960 and to date service has not been commenced by either country. Israel: A bilateral air agreement with Israel was signed February 10, 1971 with CP Air and El A1 Israel Airlines operating comparable services since March 1971.

The House resumed, from Tuesday, November 6, consideration of Bill C-132, to provide for the review and assessment of acquisitions of control of Canadian business enterprises by certain persons and of the establishment of new businesses in Canada by certain persons, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and motions Nos. 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to Bill C-132, to control foreign ownership in Canada, I followed with much interest the remarks made yesterday evening, especially those of the minister and members of the Conservative Party. Although I listened intently to the members of the Conservative Party, for the life of me I could not figure out their position on this bill. Many said that the bill went too far, and a number of others said it did not go far enough. Over the past month in this House I have noticed that the Conservative Party speaks with many voices and it is hard to understand their position.
I asked a member of the Conservative Party how a new member finds out what that party's position is. He said that their lead-off speaker is the official spokesman for the party and that he voices party policy. With regard to this bill, Mr. Speaker, we have two critics, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), and they do not agree.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: How do you know; neither of us has spoken?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
The minister looked at our amendments and rejected some very crucial ones. Later I should like to go into his arguments and comment on them, as well as some of the Conservative amendments. We proposed amendments to this bill with a view to strengthening it because we find that it does not go far enough in certain areas. The minister tried to give us the impression last evening that he is concerned about foreign ownership in this country and that he would look at some of our amendments and accept them. Our amendments are based on what is happening in this country with regard to foreign investment.
For years the opinion has been held by many Canadians and many members of this House that foreign investment is a blessing and will always be so. I agree, Mr. Speaker, that in the past as a developing country Canada did need foreign investment, but the position has changed. Look at what foreign investment has done over the years. Although it has provided some jobs for Canadians, it has developed the kind of economy that is now working in the interests of the multinational corporations rather than in
Foreign Investment Review Act the interests of the Canadian economy and the Canadian worker.
When we look at the pattern of foreign investment in this country, we see that it is mainly oriented toward resource industries and exploiting our raw materials for the benefit of another country which will refine and process them. If we become locked into that kind of economic development, not only do we export resources but we export jobs because the job-intensive areas of an economy are where the raw materials are refined and manufactured. That is not what is happening in Canada. As we ship our iron ore, pulp and other minerals out of the country we are exporting both resources and jobs. One has only to consider the oil and energy crisis today to know what that means. We are now locked into the position of a shortage of oil because of a resource-based philosophy of exporting oil via pipeline to the United States rather than having a pipeline that would be reversible and would bring western oil to eastern Canada or vice versa if need be.
Because we depend so much on foreign investment, we have been in the position of having economic decisions made outside the country. In the second reading debate I gave detailed examples of . how American corporate laws apply to industries in Canada and how American corporations' policies have caused closure of branch plants in Canada when an industry slackens in the United States in order to protect American workers as opposed to Canadian workers. I do not intend to go into any further detail on that matter.
Mr. Speaker, I think we also need to toughen this bill because of the other disadvantage related to foreign investment. So much of the research and development for subsidiary companies in Canada is done outside this country that our young scientists and engineers are losing jobs. If the branch plants were Canadian-owned, or at least were forced to do some of their research and development in this country, then jobs would be available. In 1970 alone we lost 882 engineers and scientists from Canadian universities; they went to the United States because jobs in research and development were not available with subsidiary companies in Canada. When we look at our trade balance we find that most of the component parts that foreign subsidiaries use in Canada come from other countries; parent companies provide 70 per cent of the components used by their subsidiary companies. This reduces the number of jobs created in Canada for the production of components.
When we look at the other aspect of foreign investment in this country we see that the bill could be strengthened by following some of this party's amendments. Canadian companies have been bought up at the rate of 170 a year, and there are loopholes that will allow this to continue. I shall deal with them in detail, Mr. Speaker, when I deal with the amendments. We now find that because of foreign investment we export more money than we bring in. The old argument for foreign investment was that we needed foreign capital. One has only to look at the statistics to see that between 1960 and 1969 we had a net export of $2 billion. In other words, taking into account the amount of capital that enters the country as opposed to the amount that went out in dividends and profits, we ended

This is a most crucial bill. If the minister is really serious about doing something with respect to foreign investment in this country, he should know that he will not accomplish his aim by accepting the bill as it now is. He should re-examine it and accept some of our amendments. I urge all hon. members of the House who really believe in the Canadian economy and in the Canadian ability to move ahead and plan our future to look seriously at our amendments and accept them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to take part in the debate on the report stage of Bill C-132 let me first put on record the title of the bill. According to the order paper, it is "an act to provide for the review and assessment of acquisitions of control of Canadian business enterprises by certain persons and of the establishment of new businesses in Canada by certain persons".
The amendments which I shall discuss deal with consultation with the provinces and, of course, certain notice to the provinces. I might say that in dealing with the control of our economic environment in Canada the subject is not an easy one to discuss. It is not a matter about which one can be glib. All of us agree that Canadians must control their economic destiny if they are to maintain and sustain their national identity and national sovereignty. I use the phrase "national sovereignty" in the context of our approach to national and international affairs.
How is this to be accomplished? Can we accomplish it and still maintain our standard of living? The answer to these two important questions will differ not only as between parties in this House but as between members who make up the various parties in the House. I have said before in this House that the differences between the men and women in the House stem not so much from differences in party philosophy as from regional differences. For example, members from the Maritimes discuss the problems of the Maritimes and how certain amendments to a bill will affect the Maritimes. I say again that differences in viewpoint stem not so much from party affiliation as from differences in the regions which the various members represent.
Today I wish to discuss a matter pertaining to my home province, Alberta, and to Calgary. The whole economy of Alberta is geared to ranching. That includes farming of all kinds. That industry, really, is our primary industry. Our second most powerful industry is the resource industry which brings about the secondary industries, known as the tertiary industries, all of which depend on the two main industries, farming on the one hand and the resource industry on the other, or energy and food. We in Alberta are fortunate enough to produce both food and energy in large quantities. I shall deal for a few minutes with energy.
I do not believe, and I hope I will be able to prove this before I am through, there is actually a shortage of energy in Canada. We in Alberta have enough crude petroleum and natural gas to supply the needs of Canada this winter and for winters to come. One of the great troubles has been lack of planning, particularly by this government, in the transportation of that energy from its source to urban
Foreign Investment Review Act
and other centres. I will have something more to say about that later. When we wrap it up, it may be a case of scarcity on the market but not scarcity at the wellhead.
When dealing with this subject we have to ask ourselves a second question. How do we encourage more Canadian dollars into our two industries, agriculture and the resource industry? These are some of the suggestions that I have. I have said this before in this House but the government has paid very little attention to it in dealing with the question of taxation. First, we should make certain the Canadian tax law that affects agriculture and the resource industry is such that enough dollars will be left in the command and control of people in Alberta and, indeed, the people of all Canada so they can invest in their own industries.
The new tax act places the Canadian investor in Canada at a disadvantage to foreign investors. We hear a lot about United States dollars in Canada. We hear very little about the amount of money that Japan has now invested in Canada. We hear very little about the amount of German money invested in Canada. I am told that Japanese money is coming into the Pacific coast for the hotel industry, and so on. Too often when dealing with this subject we speak about American dollars. It may be because there seems to be a group in Canada that is anti-American. If they can use a club on them, even through this bill, they seem to get great satisfaction.
There appears to be in the House panic and a crisis with regard to the supply of crude petroleum and natural gas. I repeat, there is no shortage. It is a question of transportation. We have interrogated this government since 1968 in reference to a national energy policy, transportation and pipelines, but nothing is done until there is a crisis. When this government, which is now withering on the vine, was elected in 1968 they said they were pragmatists. They are pragmatists. They go from crisis to crisis. If anyone is cold in his bed or living-room this winter, the responsibility will be on the shoulders of the government.
Guaranteeing large Canadian participation in the development and ownership of Canada can only be done by equitable and reasonable tax incentives so that Canadian developers and the resource industry can compete with foreign investors. Let me direct my attention for a few moments to the resource industry in Alberta which is continually under attack by this government and the people who like to kick hell out of the United States because it sounds good on the hustings and is more political than logical and sensible. First, I want to refer to the source of funds for independents. Resource industries, Canadian corporations and Canadians must be given, within Canada, a greater tax advantage and incentive than our foreign competitors. Then Canadians will soon own and control their resource industry and resource development.
I listened to my friends on the left who joined the government. They endorsed the new tax bill. When foreign investors come into this country, they have large depletion allowances and large write-offs. The same does not apply to Canadian investors. I recall a bill that was brought in not too long ago which permitted pipeline companies and other corporations to drill wells, but individuals forming a syndicate in Canada who might want to put their savings

November 7, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act into drilling a well cannot get even the same allowances or incentives as Canadian-owned corporations. That kind of tax law is drying up the funds for the development of our resource industries. Because of the high degree of risk inherent in the search for oil and natural gas, funds required by exploration companies cannot be borrowed.
Why, I might ask, have American dollars found their way into the resource industry? You cannot go to the bank and get a mortgage to drill an oil or gas well. Out of every ten wells drilled in the province of Alberta for oil and gas, I am told that nine are dry. Any capital that finds its way into the resource industry is high-risk capital. That is why tax incentives are necessary such as higher depletion allowances and higher write-offs. These will encourage free enterprise-I am not afraid to use that expression-to drill for oil and gas.
If it had not been for American dollars which came into Alberta and brought in Leduc No. 1 and developed the first field, there perhaps would not be any oil and gas industry in Alberta. I do not say that as a complaint. We did not find that the people of eastern Canada, who have the large pools of capital, came forward in the forties and fifties to invest in our resource industry. Therefore we had to rely on foreign investment. That is how foreign investment gained control of the resource industry of Alberta.
I want to compliment a government that was defeated by the Conservative Party, the government of Premier Manning. This is where you can differentiate from Saskatchewan. When the leases were let to developers, that government set up a royalty system which was copied by other provinces, including the province of Saskatchewan when Mr. Douglas was premier, whereby pools of money found their way into the treasuries. Because of those agreements and plans made by our former premier, now a senator, Alberta is the only province without a sales tax. We are proud of that record. We have to take that into consideration when dealing with this bill.
As one who was born in western Canada, I would be very happy if all the dollars in all our resource industries were Canadian. The only way to get Canadian dollars in there is to have an incentive and taxation plan to leave the money with Canadians. Unfortunately, that has not been the plan of this government. In history they will be written up as a giveaway and high tax government. I hear my socialist friends groaning. They ought to groan, because while we are drilling for oil and gas in Alberta and developing our resources, the same drilling rigs left Saskatchewan because of the socialistic philosophy of its government during that period.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
I am glad to hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) say "Shame". As a general rule, Canadian independents do not have sufficient internal cash flow to undertake required exploration programs. They must rely on the continued inflow of new risk capital from investors, both Canadian and foreign, either through the form of new equity issues or through drilling fund types of arrangements. It is estimated that in excess of 50 per cent of the funds expended on wildcat drilling in Canada by independents

come in the form of new risk capital obtained each year by the independent companies.
There is a need for consistency of government policies. According to recent technical papers, Canada, at current rates of production, is considered to have undiscovered reserves equivalent to 100 years of supply for oil needs and 250 years of supply for gas needs. In addition, the Alberta tar sands are estimated to contain 250 billion barrels of oil, of which 26.5 billions barrels are recoverable by current processes. As I see it, the government is bound to depend on foreign crude because it has scared off the parties ready to participate in the great Syncrude project or, if it has not, only the integrity of the government of Alberta has saved the situation. Without consultation, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) imposed a surtax, first of 40 cents and then of $1.90.
We know from all the reports on the Syncrude project that the extraction of the oil is an extremely expensive process. The cost of processing and extraction is very high. The move the government has made will, I am sure, hamper the prospects of development. I remind hon. members that we should be considering not only our present needs but Canada's needs in the future. Foresight and vision are required, and these qualities cannot be exercised without capital. On November 5 I directed the following question to the minister:
In view of the cabinet leak to the effect that the government intends to nationalize or is considering nationalizing one of the corporate parties to the Syncrude project, is the minister now in a position to encourage or to discourage the immediate development of the Syncrude project to assure supplies of crude petroleum for all Canadian needs now and in the future? That is the question today; we are all talking about supply.
To which the minister replied:
I should like to confirm a statement made outside the House, namely, that a Globe and Mail report of a proposal to acquire either Gulf or Shell is totally without foundation.
At this point an hon. member, not named in the report, interjected "Oh, yeah?" The parties to the Syncrude agreement are Imperial Oil, Canada-Cities Service Limited, Atlantic Richfield and Gulf (Canada) Limited. At the same time, it does seem strange to me that a newspaper as well-known nationally and internationally as the Globe and Mail would print a story unless there was some foundation for it. I believe there is a fight going on in cabinet at the moment over that situation. In such a climate of uncertainty, how can we be assured that a development so important to Canada's future will continue in order that our energy reserves may be maintained? The minister went on to say:
With regard to the Syncrude position, I would point out that it is a rather fundamental matter of taxation policy whether a special change should be made in our taxation law affecting the Syncrude project, and this is a matter which the Department of Finance now has under study.
Well, I hope it does not keep it under wraps for years like the government's national energy policy. This project cannot wait. It is very well put together. Eventually, 60 per cent of the profits will go to the people of Alberta. And I should like to remind hon. members, especially those from Ontario, that we spend between $100 million and $200
November 7, 1973

million a year buying from the tertiary industries of Ontario. These huge amounts are spent in the purchase of steel, tubing, facing and all the other equipment required to drill for oil and maintain the wells. We should remember, too, that if it is kept healthy this is an industry which will help solve the problems of unemployment in the future.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said no tax incentives had been provided in connection with the project. Some hon. members interjected with cries of "oh!" and then the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) answered:
Mr. Speaker, both the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and I said to the Alberta ministers that it was in the interest of this country that the Syncrude project go forward. The problem is not only how to reconcile the Syncrude project, or the agreement between the consortium and the Province of Alberta, with the existing tax laws, but of developing and announcing guidelines for federal tax resources policy. To that effect we are reviewing our position and, indeed, in the light of information supplied to the Alberta ministers, they are also reviewing their position. I will be meeting with the Syncrude people later this month.
The ministers from Alberta were down here. They visited the appropriate ministers of this government. They had hardly got on the plane home and taken off their coats before a new tax of $1.90 was imposed. What effect did that action have on the prospects for development? I see the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) present in the chamber. I understand he will speak later and I hope he will answer some of these questions. The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Bawden) put it very well, I thought, as reported at page 7515 of Hansard. He said:
In view of the fact that the only secure source of oil supply to Canada must lie in the Canadian oilfields and that Canadian oil reserves at present are down to somewhere in the order of a 12-year life, will the minister say why all the government's recent policies have aggravated the Canadian oil supply problem and why no consideration has been given to security of future supply by way of stimulating the search for and development of energy reserves in Canada?
My comment is this: you can only stimulate the search for more energy and the development of more energy through appropriate tax incentives operating in a proper atmosphere. The minister began his answer by saying he would not accuse the hon. member for Calgary South of a conflict of interest in the situation. I assume he said that because the hon. member for Calgary South was at one time an entrepreneur in one of the drilling companies. I might say, in passing, that 95 per cent of the drilling companies in Alberta are owned by Canadians, financed by Canadians and drilled on behalf of Canadians. The minister went on:
I would point out that in July and again in discussions the government has held with the governments of both Alberta and Saskatchewan we have pointed out that substantial funds can and will be made available for the purpose of developing non-conventional sources of oil particularly and, in addition, for the development of other sources of oil and natural gas, and it is our intention to have this development by and for Canadians.
The hon. member for Calgary South went on to ask a further question:
The minister has made some vague statements about the federal government trying to find ways of directing the $70 million a month that is being creamed from the western provinces into heavy oil development. In view of the fact that the National Energy Board projects production from the Alberta tar sands in
Foreign Investment Review Act the amount of some 500,000 barrels a day by 1980, which is an almost impossible target date, will the minister promise that before the end of this year the matter will be concluded so that private enterprise can get on with this job?
This is why there is an energy crisis today. It is because we have a government which believes in high taxation, a government which believes it can handle other people's business better than they can. The other day we asked the minister whether it was his intention to set up a national oil corporation. I think this was two days ago. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said later that the idea was being considered. Are they going to take over some of the companies in Alberta?

speechtext:
I thank hon. members. Continuing his answers to questions on November 5, the minister replied:
I think it would be desirable to conclude it as soon as possible and I look forward to early conversations with the government of Alberta in an attempt to nail this down.
Mr. Speaker, the government of Alberta must be frightened to negotiate with the federal government. On the last occasion when the ministers left for the west, no sooner had they done so than the whole plan was changed. I want hon. members to consider this question carefully. If the development had not taken place in Alberta, where would Canada be this winter? It would be depending entirely on supplies of oil from Venezuela and from the Middle East, where the trouble is.
In the past year the government has done everything in its power to discourage the development of the industry. While the potential reserves postulated by the various geologists are large, they will only become a reality as a result of exploration. Only through risk exploration can Canada become assured of a lasting supply.
In undertaking this risk exploration, it must first be recognized that compared to Middle East supplies, or in fact any other reserves worldwide except those of the United States, Canadian oil and gas are high-cost in terms of finding, developing and transportation costs. This is why energy is an expensive item. Some of our wells produce only 100 barrels a day, where the same sized wells in the Near East may produce 10,000 barrels a day. Yet it takes the same capital to sink the same kind of shaft. You are dealing not only with high-risk capital but with high-risk projects.
Secondly, it must be recognized that these risk investments are generally of a fairly long-term nature, in that there is a long lead time before an idea is transformed into reserves and possible return. In settled Canada, it probably takes five to seven years to do the necessary geological and geophysical work and the drilling required to develop a specific play and start selling oil and gas. In the frontier areas the lead time is even longer.

November 7, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
Gas was found at Sable Island in 1967, the year before this government took office. Close to 70 wells were sunk. Six years later this gas is still a considerable way from being produced and transported. Is this foresight? Is this the kind of government thinking and government direction that is going to guarantee us an energy supply? Of course it is not.
Gas was found at Drake Point in the Arctic in July, 1969, and it is unlikely that any gas from there will be marketed before the 1980s, if at all. Day after day I personally, as well as other members from Alberta and western Canada, have asked the Prime Minister and various ministers of energy, mines and resources whether they are negotiating with the United States to build a pipeline down the Mackenzie delta. During the last election it was almost built, with a highway alongside. We have action on the hustings but inaction in parliament.
The industry needs to work in a climate of relatively stable legislative and regulatory conditions. It cannot operate in a legislative vacuum, under conditions where great uncertainties exist, or in circumstances where legislative or regulatory guarantees are unilaterally changed without regard to the guarantee, or where legislative changes are made retroactively, or where legislative changes are quickly made without allowing for a phase-in period to allow industry adjustments.
I do not trust any government-and this is what I worry about in connection with this bill-to be the determining factor regarding where and when money should be invested, particularly in the resource industries where risk money is needed. Here I quarrel with my friends the socialists. They say that we can improve the bill. When they drilled the first well in Alberta, they took a chance. They drilled many wells at Turner Valley and other areas and finally they found oil. After finding one field they took further chances and made other discoveries and went from field to field. In this way you develop your pools of energy.
Has the government the vision to do this with taxpayers' money? That is the thought that I want my good friends to my left to think about when they talk of a national corporation that will be financed with the taxpayers' money. We talked today about CMHC and the fact that the government has been putting its hands in the taxpayers' pockets. Even though there is corruption, you cannot clean it out. Do we want the same thing to happen in the resource industry, particularly when it relies on risk capital?
If Alberta had depended on certain Toronto or Montreal investors, we would have no surplus of oil and gas today in Alberta. Those investors preferred to invest elsewhere. That was their privilege and their right, and they developed one of the greatest industrial triangles anywhere in the world. I am told that the industrial triangle of Ontario is one of the most wealthy areas anywhere in the world. Ontario has built within 100 years a powerful industrial base, and they are to be congratulated for that. I find no fault with them for not coming west and putting their money in our gas and oil wells. But had we not had money from elsewhere, there would not be the gas and oil wells in Alberta today to supply energy to the industries of eastern Canada.

speechtext:
I might say this, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to argue with my good friend who rose, but I must be saying something that bothers him or he would not want to turn off my voice.
We are developing a strong energy base. I say that what makes confederation is to have Ontario and Alberta scratching each other's backs. I hope this government does not try to stimulate an election issue by leaving the impression that instead of scratching each other's backs they are scratching each other's eyes. The energy pool complements the industrial pool. I hope that Canada's nationalism does not boil down to the price of a barrel of crude petroleum.
What do I mean by that? When we could import crude petroleum from the Near East and Venezuela and we had the Ottawa Valley division line, with imported oil coming as far as that and west of the Ottawa Valley being supplied with oil from Alberta and Saskatchewan and other places where resources industries were developed, they did not want a pipeline. Now there is a shortage, they do want a pipeline.
I say on behalf of the people I represent-and I have represented the province of Alberta in this House for 14 years-that they take the position of Canada first for Canadians. We think we are part, and a big part, of Canada and have a great contribution to make to this nation. That is why I support the amendment. We believe that this all-powerful government-it is really a majority government; both parties are together-surely could consult with the provinces and give them sufficient notification. I should not like to hand over our resource industry, financed by high-risk capital, to a government that says, "No, you cannot put money into Alberta; we don't like their premier or their government". I like a society that is governed by laws rather than by people. I am frightened when people make decisions that are made outside the rule of law. This is why I think our amendment should be supported, and I ask the government to take a hard look at it because it is to the government's advantage.
The government put a surtax on our crude petroleum. What would have been the reaction if they had put a
November 7, 1973

surtax on steel in Ontario, or on Ford or General Motors' cars? What would happen if the resources of some other province were taxed, such as the good province of Quebec or the maritime provinces? Why was poor old western Canada picked out? I say this because our resource industry and our wheat and cattle industries have been discriminated against.
I might say that not only Alberta but Saskatchewan also is losing millions of dollars through the tax. I am surprised that the Premier of Saskatchewan has not spoken up about that. Is it because there is some relationship between the party national leader and himself? I do not know.
To be fair to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, I must say that he said Ontario did buy our crude when it was more economic to purchase it elsewhere. Ontario did that for years. Everywhere west of the Ottawa Valley really did pay more. That was worked out as the national oil policy. It was introduced by a Conservative government and carried on by the Pearson government and by the present government.
Recent actions by the Canadian government have created uncertainties in the petroleum industry which may erode its ability to attract sufficient capital for the longer range development of oil and gas in Canada. Policies should be developed to provide consultation between the federal government, the provincial government and the petroleum industry, and to establish a political climate conducive to the reinvestment of funds generated from the production of our remaining proven assets of oil and gas, and as encouragement for new investments in the development of oil sands projects, exploration plays and technological research into recovery methods.
As I said, we are reluctant to the turning over of our risk capital to a group who will oppose our interests. Nor do we want to operate in a climate where it is harmful for the country to have U.S. dollars but investment by the Japanese is not questioned. Here I would also mention West Germany and Britain. Just remember that companies like the Ford Company of Canada and General Motors are under the control of the United States, but I never hear our friends in the NDP complain. Maybe the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) does not want to rock the boat in his constituency in that regard.
I am told by the hon. member for Calgary South that the Canadian Association of Oilwell Drilling Contractors is comprised of 187 companies-83 contractor companies, and 104 service, supply and manufacturing companies related to drilling operations. Member companies employ 10,000 taxpaying Canadians, providing an annual payroll in excess of $90 million to employees located throughout Canada. As a direct result of drilling operations in Canada, an annual payroll of $188 million is generated for drilling and service rig crews, employees in manufacturing, service, supply, transportation, construction, and for field consultants. Contractor members of the association are 95 per cent Canadian-owned and operate 341 drilling rigs and 205 service rigs.
Any reduction in exploration or development drilling has an immediate and adverse impact on the number of
Foreign Investment Review Act persons employed in the contracting industry. When drilling rigs are not operating, income is not generated and personnel are laid off. We know that the Syncrude project will give immediate employment to an estimated 10,000 Canadians. That is how important this industry is to Canada. Oil and gas well drilling has been carried out in every province, including the Territories and the Arctic, within the past year, creating jobs in these regions and adding economic benefit to the local, provincial and federal economies.
I am concerned that recent federal policies in respect of the crude oil price freeze and the imposition of an export tax on petroleum have created uncertainties in the Canadian petroleum industry. Today a question was asked by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) as to whether exports to the United States would be cut off in the event that supplies were not enough for Canada. The minister replied that certainly exports would be reduced in such circumstances. I endorse that. I think the industry endorses it. But at the same time, Mr. Speaker, when those decisions are made, either with the provinces or with our neighbour to the south surely consultation is not out of the question. Surely we are neighbourly enough to go to the United States and say, ' We are having our troubles." Negotiations could then take place in an atmosphere of good will on both sides of the border.
While I am vitally concerned with the maintenance of a viable drilling industry and the retention of our highly skilled Canadian labour force, I am also deeply concerned that the application of the recent policies will severely limit the discovery of additional hydrocarbon reserves, to the long-term detriment of all Canadians. I would hope that the minister or the Prime Minister would sit down and consult with the provinces before making any longterm decisions. They announced a pipeline. Quebec said no. Surely they should have first gone to Quebec and talked it over. The government has a national responsibility to supply energy across the country, but it also has a national responsibility to keep confederation together.
Our proposed amendments will tidy up a very bad bill, a bill which will cause the drying up of risk capital, capital that is necessary for the economic health of the provinces, of my province in particular, and of other provinces which depend on it for the energy they use in the manufacture of goods and the provision of services.
