speechtext:
Therefore we have government by rumour, presumably, or by any other kind of speculation. The hon. member certainly illustrates how weak are the bases of many of his arguments when he says the minister is not to be believed because the Globe and Mail says it is not true. I call attention to the fact that that newspaper did not go that far in assuming they were omnipotent and omniscient in that regard. In fact, I will send the hon. gentleman a large package of clippings of items which have appeared in the Globe and Mail and which appear every day under the heading "Our mistake."
Lest I fall victim to the temptation to try to respond in detail to what was essentially a legitimate but of course special pleading on the hon. member's behalf in regard to the oil industry, I return to my first theme. I feel my responsibility is to talk about what is a legitimate problem in all of the underdeveloped regions of Canada with regard to this whole question of investment of a foreign nature or non-Canadian nature.
I have read with considerable interest the comments made not only before the parliamentary committee but also those of some of the premiers of the Atlantic provinces-I believe they were all aligned on these things- and those of certain of the other so-called have-not provinces who expressed some fears and concerns about the possibility, or at least the threat or the danger that a more positive national policy with regard to control and ownership might be harmful to their developmental efforts.
As someone who comes from one of those have-not regions of the country and who has spent a great many years involved in various forms of developmental activity, I appreciate this concern. I have no hesitation in saying that it is important in those have-not regions of the country that legitimate developments are not hampered by a

failure of Canadian capital and Canadian initiative. I would rather put it in that context than say it would be important that these fail because there is no foreign investment. I should like to develop that point as I go along, Mr. Speaker, but before I do let me point out to people who are so very much concerned about the threat of foreign ownership in the underdeveloped parts of the country that even in these have-not areas it has been a mixed blessing to have such a heavy emphasis on foreign control and investment in industry.
In the region that I know best, the Atlantic provinces, the whole area-all four provinces-are littered, quite literally, with the remnants of foreign-eontrolled industries that milked the region for whatever they could get out of it and then departed and left us to clean up the mess.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
I have merely to point to the iron mines of Belle Isle or to Devco Corporation which was established in Cape Breton when a foreign-eontrolled organization abruptly decided to withdraw. I could give many other examples throughout Atlantic Canada of this danger that has existed all along, of the domination of the economy of the Atlantic provinces and other have-not regions by foreign-eontrolled corporations. To those who would say, in what has now become something of a cliche, that we have to embrace developers and entrepreneurs from wherever they come in the world simply because they hold out some hope of development of our resources, I say that they ought to qualify that against this history.
There is another reason why even in the have-not areas of this country it is not always wise for us to welcome every foreign investor who comes along.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Like Joey Smallwood.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: My hon. friend from Calgary North says, "Like Joey Smallwood." Well, I do not use it in the same context as he, but I would say that the Newfoundland experience in the first 20 years of confederation shows that in your enthusiasm for development you can frequently be too generous in the concessions that are made.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
I repeat, therefore, that the whole question of development has to be measured in terms of what the trade-offs are, because you could wind up making enormous concessions with insignificant benefits to the people of the region or of Canada as a whole.
The third reason this whole question of open-handedly accepting foreign investment ought to be examined is the fact that experience shows that it sometimes leads, particularly in the have-not regions, to excess interprovincial or interregional competition. This, of course, reflects on the second reason that I gave, which is that in those kinds of circumstances the promoter can play one against the other. The only winner in the long run, in many instances, is the promoter. The ultimate loser is probably the public purse which comes in and tidies up after the cream has been skimmed by those people who have no further interest in Canada or Canadians.
November 7, 1973

There is another reason why this question needs to be examined with a degree of caution. As long as we have this almost total dependence upon foreign investment in the have-not regions of the country, there is the danger, and frequently the reality, of a somewhat less than total development of the resource. The reason for this is that the international or foreign company is usually concerned with getting the basic raw material from Canada. We can see across this country, whether it be northern Ontario, Atlantic Canada, Quebec or British Columbia it does not matter, outside of the built-up regions that once foreign investment comes in the resource is usually taken out in the most raw state possible for transportation and is upgraded at some other point where the jobs are created. We can see that not only in the mining industry but also, in my own province, in the fishing industry where the basic thrust of what might be described as an international interest is to get the raw material and process it elsewhere.
We have very short memories, Mr. Speaker, if we do not recall that as recently as three or four years ago there were two or three large international corporations that were hailed when they moved into the Atlantic provinces in the fish processing business. But they disappeared from the scene the instant the price went down to the point where it was not profitable for them, at precisely that moment, to keep going. That reminds me of the Newfoundland fish merchant, Mr. Speaker, who during the depression went into his bank and asked his banker, "What do you know about the fish business?" The banker replied that he knew nothing, to which the merchant responded, throwing his keys on the desk, "You had better start learning, because you are in it."

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Time after time foreign companies have come in at the height of a market or a demand and then provincial governments, or in some instances the federal government have found themselves caught with that expression, "You had better start learning, because you are in it." We ought to differentiate between sound foreign or international investment and those problem areas which are inevitable unless we keep a close eye out for them and unless we have an alternative.
Mr. Speaker, I have made what I hope will be recognized as jesting remarks with regard to the hon. member for Calgary North, but there is one thing about which he is absolutely right; that is, we can join hands from the Atlantic provinces to the west and say that the biggest failing, in terms of Canadian control of the Canadian economy, over the past 50 years or so has been the lack of initiative and entrepreneurship and the timidity of a great deal of Canadian capital.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
This has been one of our real errors, Mr. Speaker. It is all very well to spar back and forth in adversary debate and to talk about government policies and what they might or might not have done to maintain control of the Canadian economy. But the facts speak for themselves; the evidence is there, that indeed in what might be described as the perimeters of the country, the
Foreign Investment Review Act parts away from the heartland, there has been a woeful lack of enterprise and a woeful lack of guts on the part of well-heeled Canadian investors to do something to develop other regions of the country.
My hon. friend from Calgary North spoke of some of the things that did not happen in the west or would not have happened in the west because of the failure of Canadian investors. We can point to the Atlantic provinces or Quebec in the same way. The whole fishing industry had its genesis or growth through the interests of various foreign operators. Many of the Canadians to whom I have spoken personally on many occasions, who simply could not get themselves excited about the prospects, now that prices are about four times what they were three or four years ago are falling all over themselves to get into the business. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot blame any resident, any premier or any leader in any backward part of this country for saying that he is going to get capital wherever he can lay his hands on it. What he is really saying is, "I cannot get it from Canadian sources." So it is important that we find techniques and means by which we can induce the private sector to put money in, and perhaps we could include public moneys as well, as a means to offset this negative attitude toward the regions to which I have referred.
In summary on this point, I say that it is not merely a question of saying that we do not like an overdose, as it were, of foreign investment; I think I have shown that there are dangers in that. There is no point in making that kind of case unless you point out the other flaw, which is this: Canadians, by and large, until fairly recently at least, have not been prepared to invest as they should in their own country. Lest, by the way, that is taken as a criticism wholly and solely of what might be described as the financial establishment of central Canada, let me say that within the have-not regions of this country there is every bit as much of this chicken-hearted approach to investment in Canada as there is in the big financial centres.
There are in this day and age a lot of people in the have-not regions of this country who are making good incomes, by which I mean profit incomes, from those regions. However, time and time again, as the record shows, their investments flow back to the centre. So instead of building up the have-not regions of this country, what happens? A man makes his pile, say in the Atlantic provinces, and then decides to get into something lucrative and he invests in a venture in the good old province of Ontario. That is something for us to consider. Therefore I say it is not merely a question of criticizing lack of entrepreneurship on the part of those who might be described as the well established; we must also consider the lack of entrepreneurship of those in the regions.
Another point which worries me considerably about the present state of affairs-and we hope to be able to correct this through the policies of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion-is this: speaking in terms of regional development, whether it be undertaken by foreign investors or by Canadian investors, by established companies or by new companies, I say that it is absolutely essential that the provinces themselves and the federal government, to the extent of its involvement, are satisfied

November 7, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act that enterprises undertaken are sound and that they have a degree of viability that gives them at least a reasonable chance of success.
A few moments ago I spoke about the areas of deprivation being strewn with the failures of certain economic undertakings. Those failures have arisen because a good, hard look was not taken at each and every case and no one determined adequately whether the project could safely be put in hand with a reasonable chance of success. As long as you depend either on foreign entrepreneurship, which almost inevitably is going to be opportunist by the very nature of things, and there is nothing wrong with that, or on domestic entrepreneurship, there will be a need for us to do what we are now trying to do, work with the provinces in order to establish what are the major developmental opportunities in each of those regions and which of those opportunities has a reasonable chance for growth and development.
If I may speak in terms of the bill, let me say that the concerns which have been expressed about the concept of our working with the provinces are, in my judgment, the best assurances that can be given that this measure is not going to work against the interests of the have-not or less developed areas of the country. I point out to hon. members and to you, Mr. Speaker, that the entire regional economic expansion program, as we visualize it now, will be implemented on the basis of an agreement with the provinces. Furthermore, no enterprise will be undertaken under this plan unless it is the subject of a further federal-provincial agreement of a subordinate nature.
The implications of this are, first, that it is a commitment on our part to reinforce provincial priorities; that is, how a province uses its resources or, in the general scheme of things, how those resources are to be developed is something that the province will need to decide in the first instance. Second, once we have identified a major developmental opportunity on which we are prepared to work, the very fact that the federal and provincial governments agree on that and sign an agreement to that effect will, of course, be as strong an assurance as you can get that that enterprise is going to be acceptable within the criteria set down in this bill.
As I am not aware of many, if any, provincial undertakings that have not involved in one way or another some type of federal involvement, some type of federal financial contribution, it seems to be axiomatic that the more major developmental opportunities of any significance that are covered by this bill will be ones in which the federal government will have not only a strong commitment but will require a considerable amount of federal contribution.
The hon. member for Calgary North referred to Alberta. What he said sounded familiar, as I have had the same sort of experience with other provinces as well. There is no reluctance so far as the federal government is concerned to discuss these matters with the provinces. Furthermore, it seems to me that 99 times out of 100 the shoe is on the other foot. I have never yet heard any member get up in this House and say he was deeply upset because some province had moved unilaterally. Yet I can say to hon. members that it has been my experience, and I am sure this is true of many of my colleagues, to hear on the radio or television, or read in newspapers even as reliable as the

Globe and Mail that a province has taken a significant initiative involving the federal government but has not bothered to advise us that it was even contemplating such a step.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Let us remember, therefore, that this is a two-way street. Furthermore, let me say this. I doubt very much if there is an exception to this well established rule involving federal-provincial relations. Let a province start out on its own on that project and, regardless of its feelings about wanting to act alone, or regardless of its feelings of wanting to wrap the whole thing up in a provincial package, within a few months that province will be here knocking on the door of some federal department. This applies, for instance, to Alberta with its oil development, to Quebec with its steel development, to Nova Scotia with regard to its development of deep water ports and to Newfoundland with regard to its fisheries plan. Say what you like, I think it can be recognized that the provinces recognize the necessity of doing these things in some federal context.
We, for our part, are glad that this is so because it seems to me that without some kind of overview which only the federal government, only the federal parliament, can provide not only will Canada become a balkanized country but there will be so many economic distortions in the total scheme of things that only the federal government will be able to extricate all kinds of subsidiary provincial undertakings, wherever they may be, from their difficulties. The provinces may not be able to extricate such undertakings for themselves, naturally. So the underpinning to my own approach to regional economic expansion and development is that this must be done in total concert with the provinces, but not with their imposing measures that would be harmful to our objectives. We are really saying to them, "Tell us what you want and we will try to put a federal input into it, in our attempt to make it successful."

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: It will not work.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
An hon. member says that it will not work. I say to you that if it will not work, confederation is in a heck of a sight more trouble than I think it is. This has to be made to work. I am very pleased with the co-operation we have had from provinces with regard to general development agreements and the identification of major developmental opportunities. I repeat, because I think this is essential to the concerns which have been expressed, that by working with us through these agreements in order to develop the various economic prospects in the regions of Canada, the provinces are given strong assurance that provincial interests and provincial rights will be taken into account.
I am not suggesting, of course, that this is the whole answer. I am not saying that regional economic development will solve all the economic and all other difficulties in this country; that would be naive and would be flying in the face of history. However, I do not think there is the slightest doubt that we can get a great deal more Canadian investment into the underdeveloped parts of this country. This will not necessarily be done through tax policies and the like, although these have their place, or through trans-
November 7, 1973

portation policies. We have been tinkering with these for 50 years.
The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) is mumbling something. We have now put it at the stage where we have 50 per cent of the freight rates, for instance, on manufactured goods coming out of Atlantic Canada. If we put it at 100 per cent, it would not be the total solution to the problem unless we did other things as well.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Therefore, while these one-dimensional solutions may be appealing in the long run and may be great things on the stump in an election, they nevertheless ignore the fact that if we are going to get development in the perimeters of this country, the slow growth regions- and that constitutes by far the bulk of our geography- and if we are going to ensure there is a greater Canadian input into this kind of development, we must take a multi-dimensional approach. That, I believe, is what members will see the Departmentof Regional Economic Expansion doing. I believe it is in complete concert with the bill now before the House.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the minister a short but serious question. I was impressed with some of the minister's comments about the underdeveloped areas of this country. In view of the fact Canadian banks and financial institutions lend half of their money to foreigners either in Canada or outside the country, and 38 per cent of our Canadian mutual funds are invested in the United States, I wonder whether the minister, to achieve some of his ends, would recommend foreign exchange controls or some mandatory investment controls, so that the banks and financial institutions would be required to invest more of their money in Canada and perhaps more in the areas which really need it. I would like to hear the minister's comments on this suggestion.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is obvious I cannot answer all of the implications of that question in short order. I can say this. If our federal system permits it in some way or another, I believe we have to find some means to make capital more available. For the past several months we have been carrying on a study to discover whether in fact it is true there is a shortage of capital from the lending institutions in the slow growth regions. At the moment we are getting some rather conflicting stories.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES

I think if I had said that off the top of my head, the hon. member would have asked how I could say something like that without having a study. In trying to answer the hon. member and not take up the time of the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Nesdoly), all I can say is that this is a matter about which we are certainly very concerned. subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES

If in a province such as Ontario, the provincial government set a priority such as the Toronto centre region plan which discriminates against regions such as northern Ontario, would the federal government take the initiative in doing the kinds of things which would give us the kind of development our people deserve?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Until I see evidence that that is so, I think the question is hypothetical. My negotiations are still going on with Ontario. I can say that I see no indication at the moment that they have a lack of interest in northern Ontario. There are, of course, some projects which we can undertake unilaterally under the incentives development act and things of this kind. There are others purely within provincial jurisdiction.
Without a specific example I could not say whether we could move on this or not. My opinion is we would not be able to do that. Nevertheless, there are tools that we have for encouraging industry and the like. If it was our conviction there were good programs and they did not conflict with provincial autonomy or the constitutional rights of the provinces, we would go ahead. subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate some of the comments made by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson). I hope his department will see fit to be a little more generous with Saskatchewan and the other have-not prairie province, Manitoba. I am getting a bit sick and tired of Saskatchewan being referred to as the poor socialist province, and all the rest. I will have more to say about that later.
I also hope that all of Saskatchewan will come under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and qualify for grants, particularly the small cities and towns which do not qualify at the present time. In this way we could start to build up Canadian equality and maybe gradually overcome some of the effects the multinational corporations have on us. I also hope that in the future this department will not hand out money too readily to foreign-owned corporations.
I listened with interest, and sometimes impatience to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) who represents Imperial Oil interests. He made an interesting speech. It was the Alberta lobby at work. I do not blame him. Yesterday the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) praised the Conservative government of Ontario. He took a swipe at Saskatchewan. I wish to quote from an article entitled "Foreign-ownership Rule Broken?" which appeared in the May 5 edition of the Financial Post.
Effective control of another sizeable financial institution has passed out of Canada-right under the noses of Ontario Premier William Davis and his cabinet.

November 7, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
It's Ontario Trust Co., the tenth largest trust company in Canada. While by no means a giant in the industry, Ontario Trust nevertheless has assets of $141 million and is an important trust and loan company in Ontario, where it does most of its business.
The article goes on to state who acquired it, who has the controlling interest, and so on. It further states:
Yet six months after control of Ontario Trust has left Canada, the Ontario government has done nothing about it, even though the change clearly violates the intention of its Loan and Trust Corporation Act. . .
One reason for Davis' lack of action, some observers surmise, may be the apparently friendly associations he and his cabinet have with the Ontario Trust group:
FP has learned that legal business generated by Ontario Trust is referred to Davis, Webb, Hollinrake, the Brampton law firm in which Davis was a partner.
It elaborates much more, but I think that is enough to indicate the gist of the article. What I am trying to say is this: very often governments and people in high places have deliberately sold Canada out to foreign interests.
A number of speakers have talked about the inefficiency of Saskatchewan's socialism. I want to remind those hon. members who have been taking potshots at socialism in our province that we own more of our province than is the case with most of the other provinces. For example, we have no natural gas problem in Saskatchewan right now because our gas resources and our distribution system are provincially owned. It has been that way for 20 years. If other provinces had adopted similar long-term plans, perhaps we would not be faced with the prospect of a fuel crisis in Canada today. We set up an auto insurance plan and used the money which flowed from it to build schools and hospitals and to help local industries, instead of exporting those funds to Winnipeg or Toronto or New York. The plan was successful and other provinces are now in the process of copying it. I believe hon. members should be reminded of this once in a while.
Several months ago there was a danger that one of the meat packing plants in Saskatchewan would pass into United States' hands. The Saskatchewan government bought a 45 per cent interest in it.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: You got sucked into it.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
An hon. member says we got sucked into it. I would point out to him that after we followed through with this plan two other Canadian companies indicated an interest in setting up packing plants in the province because we had indicated we were not interested in exporting our beef to Winnipeg and elsewhere. A lot of people say we got sucked into things, but time is proving us right. Someone mentioned the box factory, a socialist enterprise which was a complete flop. But the type of government we had in Saskatchewan between 1944 and 1964 was experimenting, and not all its experiments were successful. Some of them were flops. But over-all, the Crown corporations of Saskatchewan have earned more than they have ever lost, and they operate for the benefit of the people.
We have been accused by some hon. members to my right of not possessing much business experience, and the conclusion they draw is that we should not be talking

about the corporations. Heaven help our country if we leave the destiny of the nation strictly to businessmen and presidents of corporations. A multinational corporation is not guided by philosophical considerations or love of country. Such corporations have sold Canada down the river on more than one occasion. They have no pride in our country, no national purpose or vision. Yet this is what we need. We need a sense of direction, a sense of destiny in this country. We need a national purpose, and I think the Canadian people have lost it because we are so split up into regions and ideologies.
Multinational corporations are inhuman. They are formless figures which can break the law with impunity as, apparently, Ontario Trust did when it sold out to a foreign corporation with the help of the government of Ontario. Multinational corporations are very often beyond the laws of any nation. They know no national boundaries. They operate quite often in areas where labour is cheap, pay taxes where taxes are low, and sell when the price is right. They are able to switch their huge assets and resources from one country to another, thereby frustrating government policies and even altering the value of currency. Multinational corporations have to accept a great deal of responsibility for the inflation we face in this country as well as for some of the unemployment.
Multinational corporations have blamed labour for many things. I am not saying labour is all saint and no devil; it is a mixture of both. However, one can understand the concern which is expressed when wages received by labour increase by 7 or 8 per cent, and this is denounced as an inflationary trend, whereas salaries paid to executives in 1972 went up by 8.4 per cent-and 8.4 per cent on $100,000 represents a great deal of money, in addition to bonuses. That is one way of rewarding executives. They fly them to Hawaii and see that they get extra bonuses. In 1972 their bonuses were up by 34.2 per cent. This is something people in Canada do not often think about.
Several days ago mention was made on one of the networks of the Columbia River sell-out. I do not know when that happened, but I believe both Conservative and Liberal governments were involved. It was stated that the people who were negotiating this sell-out of the Columbia River were people involved with Canadian Pacific and Cominco. They were negotiating because it helped their own self-interests. They were not interested in Canada but in the welfare of Canadian Pacific and Cominco.
Crown corporations have come in for a lot of criticism in the course of this debate, but I believe that if properly run they can be of great benefit to the country, especially when no conflict of interest arises among the people who control them. Very often, however, conflicts of interest have arisen affecting the directors of Crown corporations. One example which comes to my mind is that of Eldorado Nuclear. I know that the directors of Eldorado Nuclear are also involved in some private companies. When Eldorado Nuclear left Great Bear Lake, it left behind equipment which I am told was worth over $1 million. They sold it to a private company for $150,000. Not only that, Eldorado Nuclear was sitting on top of a rich silver mine and did not even know it. Even more suspicious is the fact that after Eldorado moved to the Lake Athabasca area, within several years some of the key figures resigned and joined
November 7, 1973

the Echo Bay mines group and went back to the Great Bear region and became involved with this silver mine. So it is not only a question of conflict between Canadian corporations and foreign corporations. We have to be very careful, when we set up Canadian-run agencies, that there are no conflicts involving those who control these government-run agencies vis-a-vis private corporations whether Canadian-owned or American-owned.
I intend to support this bill. It is unfortunate that the government did not see fit to extend the screening process to apply to the expansion of existing foreign-owned companies. We tried to get this done, but it appears we have lost that battle. We shall wait for another day. I feel confident that some day we shall win this fight. Many nations are concerned about the whole question of foreign domination of their economies. Sweden, only 60 years ago, was controlled to the extent of 60 per cent by German and British companies. Yet I understand the government of that country has taken steps which have gradually brought back the whole of the Swedish economy into the hands of the Swedish people. It took 40 to 50 years, but they are there now.
We are not saying as a political party, as New Democrats, that we will be able to do this overnight, as it were, in a matter of two or three years. It will probably be a 50-year process. But as I said in one of my speeches earlier this year, we will wait patiently. Even the United States is getting a little concerned about the multinational corporation and foreign investment in the United States today. An interesting article appeared in the Financial Post for September 22, 1973, the headline of which is "Dark U.S. threats about foreigners buying up firms", The article reads:
Incredible as it may sound to the rest of the world, the U.S. is beginning to talk about restricting foreign investment in its own country.
In what must rank as one of the great reversals of modern times, some U.S. Congressmen are suggesting that Canadian, Japanese and other foreigners should not be allowed unchecked freedom to enter the U.S., take over U.S. companies, and run them in their own way.
The example of the Canada Development Corp. takeover bid for a major interest in Texasgulf Inc., is being cited as the very kind of investment which poses potential dangers to U.S. jobs and contains other economic or political dangers.
One bill has already been introduced in Congress that would virtually prevent any foreigner from gaining control of any U.S. firm.
It seems to me we have been talking about this matter for the last 15 to 20 years, yet the United States, which apparently had not been plagued with this problem hitherto, is further advanced than we are and prepared to take more drastic measures than we are.
Other less extreme bills, which would nevertheless restrict and control the growth of foreign investment in the U.S. are being considered, FP was told.
I was born and raised in a have-not province. I suppose my own personal philosophy of life has been partly tempered by poverty in my younger days, though I must say that I am fairly comfortably off now. But we hear a lot of talk about welfare funds, unemployment insurance funds and everything else. As an individual and citizen of this
Foreign Investment Review Act country, I have never received a handout from any government, any province or any other person in this country, and I am proud of it. However, I am always willing to pay a few extra bucks in taxes and to give a few dollars here and there if somebody needs it, and I do not begrudge it at all. That has always been my philosophy. Canadians are selling out their own country. And worse, they are very often financing their own sell-out. If we do not reverse the trend soon, we are not going to have a Canada and my children are not going to have a Canada that we all love so dearly.
I should like to quote several paragraphs of a report of remarks made by the president of the Committee for an Independent Canada, a chap by the name of Hurtig. I was rather impressed with his ideas. I think there are some former Liberals and Conservatives in this group; it is a sort of an all-party committee. It is a pressure group, the one pressure group I listen to with interest. Some months ago he spoke to a group of teachers in the province of Saskatchewan and cited the following percentages of foreign ownership and control in Canada. Undoubtedly the House has heard these figures before. Manufacturing, 60 per cent foreign-owned; mining, 60 per cent; petroleum refining, 99.9 per cent foreign-owned-I ask my hon. friend from Calgary North to write that figure; the oil and gas industry, 83 per cent; primary metal smelting and refining, 87 per cent; the automobile industry, 97 per cent; rubber industry, 90 per cent; chemical industry, 78 per cent; the computer industry, 90 per cent; and the aircraft and aircraft parts industries, 92 per cent.
According to Mr. Hurtig, these statistics prove that Canada has a branch plant economy. With that assumption he developed the following syllogism:
A branch plant economy produces a branch plant society, which produces branch plant social values, which produce branch plant culture, which produces branch plant mentality.
This is what we have in Canada today, a branch plant mentality. Our news media, radio stations and television stations have the mentality of a branch plant. Our approach to investment has a branch plant mentality about it. Our people have no faith in their own country as a result of this branch plant mentality. It is time we took stock of our resources and made up our minds that we are going to get Canada back in the hands of Canadians. It could be done if we put our will to it.
Several years ago the government of Saskatchewan introduced legislation to prohibit foreign ownership of Saskatchewan land. There was a real outcry about it and the legislation was withdrawn, but I hope they will be bringing the bill back again. It is not only a question of foreign ownership of Saskatchewan land, but even Toronto and Vancouver ownership of our land bothers us. In one area of Saskatchewan, 50 sections of prime farmland is owned by Ontario interests. All of the profit derived from that farmland goes back to Ontario-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. On two previous occasions in the House I was not permitted to complete my remarks, so I appreciate this very much. This is a "first" for me.
Hurtig went on to say that it is not too late to do something about it, but time is running out. Unless we very soon turn our country around, and in a dramatic manner, the future of our country is in danger, he said. He claimed that in the decade from 1961 to 1971, foreigners had bought up Canada to the tune of $21 billion but only 19 per cent of that money was foreign money; 81 per cent of the amount was borrowed from Canadian sources. The article continues:
During the Trudeau years, said Hurtig, American firms sent back to the U.S.A. over $8 billion more than the entire amount of capital brought into Canada.
I believe reference to this was made earlier in our discussion. The article continues:
The sale of Ryerson Press was a specific example of Canadians financing their own sell-out, he said. The 140-year old Canadian company was sold to a U.S. firm for $2 million borrowed from a Canadian bank.
I feel the question asked by the hon. member for York-ton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) about Canadian financial institutions financing our own sell-out is very pertinent at this time.
I should like to thank the House very much for giving me extra time so I could conclude my remarks. An hon. member has sent me over a poem, but I do not think I will read it. I understand parliament is supposed to recess some time in December and there will be a new session after January 1. I hope the New Democratic Party amendments are supported by all sides of the House. We are going to oppose the Conservative Party amendments because they would weaken the bill. I also sincerely hope that as a measure of good faith in the Canadian people- this is a very important matter for them; they feel Canada must regain its own independence-this bill will pass before the House recesses.
